title: dedicated-capacity-autoscale-misfire-retrospective
content:
Summary:

On 2026-02-16 at ~15:05 UTC we observed a multi-hour degradation for several Dedicated GPU pools in us-west-2. Symptoms were increased queuing latency for customer requests routed to Dedicated, increased token p95 latency from ~220ms to ~1.8s for a subset of model routes, and several autoscaling groups failing to scale out despite steady queue depth. The degradation impacted three customers on Reserved capacity and caused partial routing fallbacks to hosted models. No data exfiltration or model corruption was observed.

Primary impact: customer-facing latency/throughput regressions; billing/credits adjustments for affected customers; manual intervention required to restore normal autoscaling.

Immediate on-call actions and timeline (abridged):
- 15:05 UTC: Pager triggered (high token p95) - oncall (Aisha) acked.
- 15:09 UTC: Confirmed p95 spike and increased queue depth on dedicated-pool-7 and -9.
- 15:15 UTC: Noticed failed scale-out events in the autoscaler logs: backoff due to "failed allocation" events from the cluster scheduler (K8s cluster autoscaler).
- 15:25 UTC: Engineers attempted a manual node-provision via infra-provisioner job; nodes started provisioning but failed health checks and were not added to node pools.
- 15:40 UTC: Identified multiple noisy neighbor pods on pool-7 causing GPU PCIe saturation metrics and OOM kills on colocated model workers.
- 16:10 UTC: Applied temporary mitigation: cordon + drain noisy pods, force scale dedicated pools down/up to reset placement; partial recovery began at ~16:35 UTC.
- 17:00 UTC: Full autoscaler config rollback (reverted a config change deployed earlier that day) and knob adjustments to allocation timeouts.
- 17:40 UTC: Monitoring returned to baseline for most routes; incident declared mitigated. Post-incident follow-ups continued over next 48 hours.

Root cause hypothesis (triaged):
1) Autoscaling misconfiguration (primary): A malformed autoscaler rollout earlier in the day (PR #1289) changed the "allocationTimeout" from 8m to 2m for Docker-based worker nodes. The shorter timeout caused the cluster autoscaler to mark provisioning attempts as failed prematurely when GPU provisioning took longer than 2m due to NVLink/NVMe initialization and driver bind time. This led to backoff and eventually prevented scale-out.

2) Noisy neighbor / placement fragility (contributor): During the period when scale-out was failing, a handful of experimental batch jobs (non-customer, internal test runs) were pinned to specific GPU hosts. Those jobs produced heavy PCIe and memory bandwidth usage, which increased GPU driver DDL latency and triggered eviction heuristics on colocated inference pods. Combined with the autoscaler backoff, this amplified queue buildup.

3) Observability blind spot: The allocation timeout metric/change was not surfaced in per-release rollout dashboards and there was no alert on repeated provisioning timeouts. Our SLI for node provisioning success rate is coarse-grained and did not trip before p95 token latency crossed customer-facing thresholds.

Evidence and logs (high-level):
- Autoscaler logs: repeated "allocation timed out after 120s" (matches PR change) and subsequent exponential backoff.
- Kubelet logs on failing nodes: slow nvidia-driver bind at ~90-150s followed by kubelet failing healthchecks.
- GPU metrics: PCIe bandwidth saturating to 95% on host gpu-32 during the high-impact window; per-pod GPU memory usage high on experimental-job-442.
- Placement controller: "insufficient resources" errors despite available physical capacity due to taints/tolerations and topology constraints.

Why the change was risky:
- The PR that altered allocationTimeout was intended to make autoscaling more responsive to provisioning failures in non-GPU node types, but it did not account for known GPU driver initialization delays. There was no gating (canary rollout) for Dedicated pools and the change reached production during working hours.

Mitigations applied during the incident (short-term):
- Drained noisy experimental pods and quarantined the internal batch job queue.
- Reverted the autoscaler allocationTimeout to 8m for affected Dedicated clusters.
- Increased autoscaler backoff threshold temporarily to allow more retries during provisioning spike.
- Manually provisioned nodes with a warm-start image (pre-loaded drivers) to speed initialization for critical pools.
- Implemented temporary routing policy to move small-percentage traffic to hosted fallback models to protect customer SLAs.

Post-incident follow-ups and planned actions (owner + ETA):
- Aisha (owner) - Immediate (within 72h): Add an alert rule for repeated allocation timeouts (>3 within 10m) and a dashboard tile showing allocationTimeout to rollout dashboards.
- Marco - 2 weeks: Harden autoscaler PR review checklist to include GPU driver init profiling and require explicit per-node-type rollout flags.
- Jordan - 1 week: Update Dedicated capacity runbook with a dedicated section "Autoscaler timeouts — GPU pools" including exact commands for temporary rollback and warm-node provisioning steps.
- Priya - 2 weeks: Add admission control to disallow experimental batch jobs from landing on Dedicated GPU hosts by default; create a namespace + taint model for internal test workloads.
- Eng infra - 3 weeks: Create an automated warm-image build that preloads GPU drivers and warms NVMe to reduce cold-start initialization time below 2 minutes for critical pools.

Runbook changes (draft text to be inserted):
- New play: "Scale-out failure on Dedicated pools"
  - Symptoms: repeated allocation timeout, queue depth rising above 200 requests, p95 tokens > 1s for > 10 minutes.
  - Quick checks: is allocationTimeout overridden? `kubectl -n infra get configmap autoscaler-config -o yaml` and check allocationTimeout.
  - Immediate actions: if allocationTimeout < 5m, revert via `kubectl -n infra patch configmap autoscaler-config -p '{"data":{"allocationTimeout":"8m"}}'` and restart autoscaler.
  - Noisy neighbor isolation: `kubectl top nodes --use-protocol-buffers` + `kubectl get pods -o wide --sort-by=.spec.nodeName` to identify heavy GPU usage. Cordon node and `kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data` for identified host, then trigger re-placement.
  - Warm provisioning: use infra job `infra/warm-node-provisioner` with `--image=warm-gpu-2026-02` (internal tool).

On-call notes / lessons learned:
- Avoid global changes to autoscaler defaults during working hours for node types with known long-init. Use canary rollouts and explicit scope flags.
- Ensure PRs that target infra components list impacted node types and include a short timing profile (expected init times).
- Improve test harness: simulate slow GPU init in staging and ensure autoscaler behavior is validated against that profile.
- Short-term: protect Dedicated pools from internal experimental workloads via namespace/taint policy.

Open action items (tracking):
- [ ] Add allocationTimeout metric + alert (Aisha) — due 2026-03-12
- [ ] Autoscaler PR checklist update + template (Marco) — due 2026-03-02
- [ ] Draft runbook section + playbook tests (Jordan) — due 2026-02-25 (in progress)
- [ ] Namespace isolation for internal batch jobs (Priya) — due 2026-03-03
- [ ] Warm node image pipeline (infra) — roadmap Q2 2026

Notes and context (informal):
- The internal batch job that was noisy was originally scheduled as a short ad-hoc stress test; it slipped into prod node selectors because the test owner reused an existing job template. We should add a preflight check that prevents job templates with GPU nodeSelectors from being run outside the "internal-test" namespace.
- Customer comms: CS drafted an initial apology and credit offer; final wording coordinated with legal. No escalations beyond account-level CSMs.

Appendix (commands observed in incident):
- `kubectl logs -n infra autoscaler-0 | grep allocation
  "allocation timed out after 120s"`
- `kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep NotReady`
- `nvidia-smi -q -d PIDS,MEMORY | grep -B3 "Process ID"`
- `kubectl cordon gpu-host-32 && kubectl drain gpu-host-32 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data`

Draft status: working doc for SRE review. Once runbook text is finalized we will push a small PR to `platform/docs/runbooks/dedicated-autoscaler.md` and schedule a short postmortem review with product/infra/CS (invite sent to relevant stakeholders).

If you have additional logs or customer traces, paste them below (use the incident thread in Slack to avoid spamming):
- slack thread: #sre-oncall thread/p16233

-- Aisha
